title: The Traitorous Eight Leave Shockley
text:
In 1956 William Shockley, co-inventor of the transistor and soon to be a Nobel laureate, set up the Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory in Mountain View, California, and recruited a group of brilliant young scientists and engineers. Among them were Robert Noyce, Gordon Moore, Jean Hoerni, Eugene Kleiner, Jay Last, Julius Blank, Victor Grinich and Sheldon Roberts.

Shockley proved a difficult boss. He was suspicious and controlling. When a secretary cut her hand on a pin, he suspected sabotage and wanted staff to take lie detector tests. He also shifted the lab's focus away from silicon transistors toward a device the young team doubted. The eight asked the lab's financial backer, Arnold Beckman, to bring in a different manager. Beckman decided to keep Shockley in charge.

So the eight decided to leave together. Kleiner wrote to an investment firm in New York, and a young banker there, Arthur Rock, helped them find a backer: Sherman Fairchild's Fairchild Camera and Instrument. In September 1957 they resigned and founded Fairchild Semiconductor. They became known as the "traitorous eight."

At Fairchild, Hoerni developed the planar process, and Noyce used it to make a practical integrated circuit. Dozens of companies were later spun off by Fairchild alumni, including Intel, founded by Noyce and Moore in 1968. Kleiner co-founded the venture firm Kleiner Perkins. Shockley's own company never succeeded.
lesson: Talent stays with a team, not a famous boss. A group that trusts each other enough to move together can achieve far more than its former leader.
people: Robert Noyce, Gordon Moore, Jean Hoerni, Eugene Kleiner, Jay Last, Julius Blank, Victor Grinich, Sheldon Roberts, William Shockley
source: Leslie Berlin, The Man Behind the Microchip (2005); Michael Riordan and Lillian Hoddeson, Crystal Fire (1997)
